newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - In search of the Europension.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - In search of the Europension.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN

Recently Proteus noted that France had become one of the most interesting markets to watch for new developments. That was triggered by merger and acquisition talk surrounding AGF and GAN. That talk has not gone away, and indeed an article in Le Monde today points out that both companies may become choice targets for European insurers aiming for growth, provided GAN recapitalisation allows it to write off its property exposure.
But now British life insurers are looking across the channel for a new market for personal pensions.

Imminent legislation is expected to allow French workers to take out personal pensions for the first time. This would create a massive potential market, and executives of UK life insurers, which already have expertise in selling these kind of products, are brushing up on their French.

Commercial Union, which already has a strong French connection through its subsidiary Groupe Victoire, intends to launch a major sales drive, and other insurers such as General Accident, Norwich Union and Standard Life, will start selling pensions there this year.
Prudential, Britain's biggest insurance company, is analysing the potential of the European pensions markets and expects to complete its research soon.

The reason behind the change of legislation is similar to that which lead Margaret Thatcher to open the private pensions market in the UK in 1988. France is in the grip of a pensions funding crisis, and with an ever increasing proportion of retired people it simply cannot afford to foot the state pensions bill for much longer.

Three observations come out of this development. First, the issue of regulation. UK life insurers got themselves in to a mess in the early 1990s when industry watchdogs discovered anomalies in the way 90 per cent of policies had been sold. While the process of sorting this out may be what UK life insurers mean when they talk about 'expertise', they will have to make sure they do not run afoul of French authorities new to regulating the sector.

Second, France is not the only European country facing the problem - there are also state pension fund shortfalls in Germany, Italy, the Netherlands and Spain. If a 'Europension' product can be developed in France, it may well lead the way for similar initiatives in these other countries.

Finally, the development could be the one which makes single Euro insurance market legislation a reality. The European Commission's Third Life and Non-life directives have had little effect so far, but the chance of selling life products, the need to rationalise regulation across the community, and the inevitable growth of a Euro non-life insurance once brand names become known across the market, could make the legislator' dream a commercial reality.
